cues.text: Section nine: testing and maintaining recovery plans.
A recovery plan is credible only when its assumptions and its recovery procedures have been tested.
A plan that has never been exercised is a set of hopes, not a capability.
Let us look at the kinds of test, one row at a time.
First, the checklist review.
Here the team verifies completeness, and checks that contacts and responsibilities are correct and assigned.
Second, the walkthrough.
In a walkthrough, the team reviews the steps of the plan and the dependencies between them.
Third, the tabletop exercise.
Participants discuss a simulated crisis, talking through what they would do, without actually changing any systems.
Fourth, the simulation.
This is a controlled exercise of selected recovery activities, so some real actions are performed, but only a chosen part of the plan.
Fifth, the parallel test.
Here the team recovers an alternate environment without stopping the primary service, so production keeps running while the recovery capability is proved.
Sixth, the full interruption test.
This is a controlled switch away from the primary service, so the organisation genuinely operates from the recovery arrangements.
Notice that the tests move from discussion and review, toward real action, and finally to real interruption.
Testing should have clear objectives, an authorised scope, safeguards, evidence, and restoration arrangements, so that normal service can be returned afterwards.
During a test, measure the actual recovery time, the data loss, the service integrity, the communications, and the quality of decisions.
Then compare the results with the RTO and the RPO, record the gaps, and assign corrective actions.
Consider an example.
A recovery exercise restores a database in 90 minutes, but loses 40 minutes of transactions.
The RTO is 2 hours, and the RPO is 15 minutes.
Ninety minutes is within two hours, so the time target passes.
But forty minutes of lost transactions exceeds the fifteen minutes allowed, so the data-loss target fails.
The corrective action is to improve replication or backup frequency, and then retest.
Finally, plans must be maintained.
Review them after major changes, after incidents, after exercises, after supplier changes, and at scheduled intervals.
Update contact lists, architecture, dependencies, and recovery procedures.
Remember that a stale plan may direct engineers to infrastructure that no longer exists.
